name: Catenary curve
seoDesc: Catenary curve: work out coordinate (x) from the sag parameter and the catenary value. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: coordinate (x) is what the Catenary curve calculator works out, and it gets there from the sag parameter, the catenary value, the weighted catenary value and the interval boundary. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Catenary curve calculator work?
sections.html:
The Catenary curve calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports coordinate (x) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of curve and the type of output); then you type in the sag parameter (a), the catenary value (y), the weighted catenary value (y) and the interval boundary.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Catenary curve calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Coordinate (x)=sag parameter (a) × (catenary value (y) ÷ sag parameter (a))
Weight parameter (b)=weighted catenary value (y) ÷ (coordinate (x) ÷ sag parameter (a))
Step=2 × interval boundary ÷ (num − 1)
Step=2 × interval boundary ÷ (numt − 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Type of curve set to Catenary, Sag parameter (a) = 1, Weight parameter (b) = 4 and Type of output set to Graph — it reports Num = 101 and Numt = 11.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Num = 101 and Numt = 11 should be roughly the size you expected from Type of curve set to Catenary and Sag parameter (a) = 1.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Catenary curve calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the sag parameter, the catenary value and the weighted catenary value — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Catenary curve calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns coordinate (x), derived from the sag parameter, the catenary value and the weighted catenary value. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Catenary curve calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the sag parameter, the catenary value, the weighted catenary value and the interval boundary, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Num = 101. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Catenary curve calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
